A person who writes what he composes in his mind; the author of a written paper or of writings; an author in general; a literary producer of any kind: as, the ''writer'' of a letter; a ''writer'' of history or of fiction.
{{smaller block|<poem>Tell prose ''writers'' stories are so stale
That penny ballads make a better sale. ''Breton.''</poem>
“I love,” said Mr. Sentry, “a critic who mixes the rules of life with annotations upon ''writers.''”

'''writhe''' (rīᴛ̵ʜ), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''writhed'', ppr. ''writhing''. [< ME. ''writhen'', ''wrythen'' (pret. ''wroth'', ''wrooth'', ''wræth'', pl. ''writhen'', pp. ''writhen'' (with short ''i''), ''wrethen''), < AS. ''wrīthan'' (pret. ''wrāth'', pp. ''writhen''), twist, wind about, = OHG. ''rīdan'', MHG. ''rīden'', G. dial. ''wrideln'', twist together, = Icel. ''ritha'' = Sw. ''vrida'' = Dan. ''vride'', wring, twist, turn, wrest. Hence ult. ''wreath'', ''wrest'', ''wrist''.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To turn and twist about; twist out of shape or position; wrench; contort.
{{smaller block|<poem>The stortes [grape-stalks] softe in handes wol thai take
And ''writhe'' hem, and so ''writhen'' wol thai lete
Hem honge and drie awhile in sonnes hete.</poem>
{{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 206.}}
<poem>Sa suld we ''wryth'' all syn away,
That in our breistis bred.</poem>
{{right|''The Bludy Serk'' (Child’s Ballads, VIII. 151).}}
The desolate little shanty was plainly to be seen among the naked and ''writhen'' boughs of the orchard.
{{right|''The Atlantic'', LVIII. 389.}}}}
'''2.''' To wrest perversely; wrest; pervert.
{{smaller block|The reason which he yieldeth showeth the least part of his meaning to be that whereunto his words are ''writhed.''
{{right|''Hooker.''}}}}
'''3.''' To wrench; wring; extort. [Obsolete or archaic.]
{{smaller block|The nobility hesitated not to follow the example of their sovereign in ''writhing'' money from them by every species of oppression. ''Scott'', Ivanhoe, vi. (''Imp. Dict.'')}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To move or stir in a twisting or tortuous manner; twist about, as from pain, distress, or stimulation.

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|writ|6993|writhe}}</noinclude>{{smaller|'''rogative writ.''' See the qualifying words.—'''Service of a writ.''' See ''service''.—'''Ship writ,''' in ''Eng. hist.'', a writ issued in the name of the crown imposing the tax known as ''ship-money'' (which see): notably one of such writs issued under Charles I. which led to Hampden’s opposition. They were declared illegal by 16 Car. I., c. 14 (1640).—'''The writ runs.''' (''a'') The writ is expressed in terms of or including: as, ''the writ runs'' in the name of the people. (''b'') The writ is legally capable of enforcement: as, ''the writ'' of subpœna ''runs'' throughout the state. (''c'') The writ is practically capable of enforcement: as, “When lawlessness has yielded to order; when the Queen’s ''writ runs;'' when the edicts of the civil courts are obeyed; . . . and when sedition is trampled under foot—then, and then only, is there some chance for the development of remedial measures.” (''Edinburgh Rev.'', CLXV. 587.)—'''To serve a writ.''' See ''to serve a process'', under ''serve''.—'''To serve a writ of attachment.''' See ''to serve an attachment'', under ''serve''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Twelve-day writ,''' in ''Eng. law'', a writ allowed by 18 and 19 Vict., c. 67, in actions on bills and notes if brought within six months after maturity, warning defendant to appear within twelve days, otherwise judgment would go against him.—'''Vicontiel writs†.''' See ''vicontiel''.—'''Writ of account.''' See ''action of account'', under ''account''.—'''Writ of assistance, besayle†, capias, certiorari, consultation, dower, error, estrepement.''' See ''assistance'', etc.—'''Writ of execution.''' See ''execution'', 3 (''b'').—'''Writ of habeas corpus, inquiry, mandamus, possession, privilege, prohibition, protection, recaption, restitution, right, spoliation, subpœna,''' etc. See ''habeas corpus'', ''inquiry'', etc.—'''Writs of extent.''' See ''extent'', 3 (''b'').}}

'''writ<sup>2</sup>''' (rit). An obsolete form of the third person singular present indicative (for ''writeth''), and an obsolete or archaic form of the past participle, of ''write''.

'''writability''' (rī-ta-bil′i-ti), ''n.''   [< ''writable'' + ''-ity'' (see ''-bility'').]   Ability or disposition to write. [Nonce-word.]

{{smaller block|You see by my ''writability'' in my pressing my letters on you that my pen has still a colt’s tooth left.
{{right|''Walpole'', Letters, IV. 455. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''writable''' (rī′tạ-bl), ''a.''   [< ''write'' + ''-able.'']   Capable of being written; such as might be set down in writing. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|The talk was by no means ''writable'', but very pleasant.
{{right|''Mme. D’Arblay'', Diary, II. 168. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''writative''' (rī′ta-tiv), ''a.''   [Irreg. (after ''talkative'') < ''writ(e)'' + ''-ātive.'']   Disposed or inclined to write; given to writing. [Nonce-word.]
{{smaller block|Increase of years makes men more talkative, but less ''writative.''
{{right|''Pope'', To Swift, Aug. 17, 1736.}}}}

'''write''' (rīt), ''v.''; pret. ''wrote'' (obs. or dial. ''wrate'', archaic ''writ''), pp. ''written'' (obs. or archaic ''writ'', formerly erroneously ''wrote''), ppr. ''writing.''   [< ME. ''writen'' (pret. ''wrot'', ''wroot'', ''wrat'', pl. ''writen'', ''write'', pp. ''writen'', ''write''—with short ''i''), < AS. ''wrītan'' (pret. ''wrāt'', pl. ''writon'', pp. ''writen''), write, inscribe, orig. score, engrave, = OS. ''wrītan'', cut, injure, write, = OFries. ''wrīta'' = D. ''rijten'', tear, split, = LG. ''riten'' = OHG. ''rīzan'', cut, tear, split, draw, delineate, MHG. ''rīzen'', G. ''reissen'', tear, = Icel. ''rīta'', scratch, cut, write, = Sw. ''rita'', draw, delineate, = Goth. *''wreitan'' (in deriv. ''writs'', a stroke or point made with a pen), write. Hence ''writ''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To trace or form upon the surface of some material (a significant character or characters, especially characters constituting or representing words); set down, in a manner adapted for reading, with a pen, pencil, style, or anything with which marks can be made; inscribe: as, to ''write'' a word on paper; to ''write'' one’s name with the finger in sand.
{{smaller block|Aboven, in the Dust and in the Powder of tho Hilles, thei ''wroot'' Lettres and Figures with hire Fingres.
{{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 17.}}}}
{{smaller block|They . . . whose names are not ''written'' in the book of life.
{{right|Rev. xvii. 8.}}}}
{{smaller block|The Greek metropolitan has a very fine manuscript of the Pentateuch, supposed to have been ''wrote'' about the year eight hundred.
{{right|''Pococke'', Description of the East, II. ii. 38.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>There is a Book
By seraphs ''writ'' with beams of Heavenly light.</poem>
{{right|''Cowper'', Sonnet to Mrs. Unwin.}}}}
'''2.''' To cover with writing; trace readable characters over the surface of.
{{smaller block|And it [the roll] was ''written'' within and without.
{{right|Ezek. ii. 10.}}}}
{{smaller block|There will she sit in her smock till she have ''writ'' a sheet of paper.
{{right|''Shak.'', Much Ado, ii. 3. 138.}}}}
'''3.''' To express or communicate in writing; give a written account of; make a record of, as something known, thought, or believed: as, to ''write'' one’s observations; he ''wrote'' down all he could remember. {{smaller|Sometimes, in this and the next sense, the verb is followed by a dative without its sign: as, ''write'' me all the news. <poem>Thanne sit he down and ''writ'' in his dotage
That wommen kan nat kepe hir mariage.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Prol. to Wife of Bath’s Tale, l. 709.}}}}
{{smaller block|Is it not ''written'', My house shall be called of all nations the house of prayer? {{right|Mark xi. 17.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>All your better deeds
Shall be in water ''writ'', but this in marble.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Philaster, v. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|I chose to ''write'' the Thing I durst not speak.
{{right|''Prior'', Solomon, ii.}}}}

'''4.''' To set forth as an author, or produce in writing, either by one’s own or another’s hand; compose and produce as an author.

{{smaller block|''Write'' me a sonnet.
{{right|''Shak.'', Much Ado, v. 2. 4.}}}}

{{smaller block|When you ''writ'' your Epigrams, and the Magnetic Lady, you were not so mad.
{{right|''Howell'', Letters, I. v. 16.}}}}

'''5.''' To designate by writing; style or entitle in writing; record: with an objective word or phrase.

{{smaller block|O that he were here to ''write'' me down an ass!
{{right|''Shak.'', Much Ado, iv. 2. 78.}}}}

{{smaller block|They belonged to the armigerous part of the population, and were entitled “to ''write'' themselves Esquire.”
{{right|''De Quincey'', Bentley, i.}}}}

'''6.''' To record; set down legibly; engrave.

{{smaller block|There is ''written'' in your brow . . . honesty and constancy.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., iv. 2. 162.}}}}

{{smaller block|The history of New England is ''written'' imperishably on the face of a continent.
{{right|''Lowell'', Among my Books, 1st ser., p. 228.}}}}

{{smaller|'''To write down.''' (''a'') To set down in writing; make a record or memorandum of.}}

{{smaller block|Having our fair order ''written down''.
{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, v. 2. 4.}}}}

{{smaller block|It was the manner of that glorious captain [Cæsar] to ''write down'' what scenes he passed through.
{{right|''Steele'', Spectator, No. 374.}}}}

{{smaller|(''b'') To write in depreciation of; injure by writing against: as, to ''write down'' a play or a financial undertaking; to ''write down'' an actor or a candidate.}}

{{smaller block|Without some infusion of spite it seems as if history could not be written; that no man’s zeal is roused to write unless it is moved by the desire to ''write down''.
{{right|''Stubbs'', Medieval and Modern Hist., p. 110.}}}}
{{smaller block|'''To write off''', to cancel by an entry on the opposite side of the account or bill: as, to ''write off'' discounts; to ''write off'' bad debts.—'''To write out.''' (''a'') To make a copy or transcription of; especially, to make a perfect copy of, after a rough draft; record in full: as, when the document is ''written out'' you may send it off. (''b'') To exhaust the capacity or resources of by excessive writing: used reflexively: as, that author has ''written himself out''.—'''To write up.''' (''a'') To bring up to date or to the latest fact or transaction in writing; write out in full or in detail: as, to ''write up'' an account or an account-book; to ''write up'' a fire or a celebration for a newspaper. (''b'') To attempt to elevate in estimation or credit by favorable writing; commend to the public; puff: as, to ''write up'' a new play or a candidate.—'''Written law.''' See ''law''<sup>1</sup>.}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To be acquainted with or practise the art of writing; engage in the formation of written words or characters, either occasionally or as an occupation: as, to ''write'' in school; to ''write'' as a lawyer’s clerk.
{{smaller block|He can ''write'' and read and cast accompt.
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., iv. 2. 92.}}}}
'''2.''' To express ideas in writing; practise written composition; work as an author, or engage in authorship.
{{smaller block|When I ''wrate'' of these deuices, I smiled with my selfe, thinking that the readers would do so to.
{{right|''Puttenham'', Arte of Eng. Poesie, p. 84.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Like Egyptian Chroniclers,
Who ''write'' of twenty thousand Years.</poem>
{{right|''Cowley'', Pindaric Odes, xii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|Herodotus, though he ''wrote'' in a dramatic form, had little of dramatic genius.
{{right|''Macaulay'', History.}}}}
'''3.''' To conduct epistolary correspondence; communicate by means of letter-writing; convey information by letter or the like: as, to ''write'' to a distant friend; ''write'' as soon as you arrive. {{smaller block|I go. ''Write'' to me very shortly.
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., iv. 4. 428.}}}}

'''write''' (rīt), ''n.''   [< ''write'', ''v.'']   Writing: chiefly in the phrase ''hand of write.'' [Colloq. or vulgar.]
{{smaller block|We trust you will call back yourself from errors and heresies advisedly which you have maintained rashly, and set forth by word and ''write'' busily.
{{right|''Harding to Jewell'', in Bp. Jewell’s Works (Parker Soc. ed.), [II. 804.}}}}
{{smaller block|It was a short, but a well-written letter, in a fair ''hand of write.''
{{right|''Galt'', Annals of the Parish, i. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''writee''' (rī-tē′), ''n.''   [< ''write'' + ''-ee''<sup>1</sup>.]   A person to or for whom something is written; a reader as contrasted with a writer. [Occasional.]
{{smaller block|And, indeed, where a man is understood, there is ever a proportion betwixt the writer’s wit and the ''writee’s.''
{{right|''Chapman'', Iliad, xiv., Com. (ed. Hooper).}}}}

'''write-of-hand''' (rīt′ọv-hand′), ''n.'' Handwriting; the art of writing. [Vulgar.]
{{smaller block|“A could wish as a’d learned ''write-of-hand,''” said she, “for a’ve that for to tell Christopher as might set his mind at ease.”
{{right|''Mrs. Gaskell'', Sylvia’s Lovers, xliii. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''writer''' (rī′tėr), ''n.''   [< ME. ''writere'', < AS. ''writere'' (= Icel. ''ritari''); as ''write'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' A person who understands or practises the art of writing; one who is able to write; a penman.
{{smaller block|My tongue is the pen of a ready ''writer.''
{{right|Ps. xlv. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' One who does writing as a business; a professional scribe, scrivener, or amanuensis: used specifically in England of clerks to the former East India Company, and of temporary copying clerks in government offices; in Scotland, loosely, of law agents, solicitors, attorneys, etc., and sometimes of their principal clerks.—'''3.''' A person who writes what he composes in his mind; the author of a written paper or of writings; an author in general; a literary producer of any kind: as, the ''writer'' of a letter; a ''writer'' of history or of fiction.
{{smaller block|<poem>Tell prose ''writers'' stories are so stale
That penny ballads make a better sale. ''Breton.''</poem>
“I love,” said Mr. Sentry, “a critic who mixes the rules of life with annotations upon ''writers.''”
{{right|''Steele'', Spectator, No. 350.}}}}
[For other uses of the word, see ''letter-writer'', 2, and ''type-writer''.]

{{smaller|'''Ship’s writer.''' See ''ship''.—'''The writer,''' the author of this writing; the writer hereof: used elliptically by a writer with reference to himself, to avoid saying ''I''.—'''Writer of the tallies.''' See ''tally''<sup>1</sup>, 1.—'''Writers’ cramp''', an occupation-neurosis occurring in those who write much, especially in a contracted hand. It affects at first usually only those muscles which are directly concerned in the production of writing movements, but, if the act is persisted in, the neighboring muscles may also share in the disturbance. The affection may manifest itself under one of four forms or a combination of them—namely, ''paralytic'', in which weakness in the fingers or even absolute inability to hold the pen is experienced; ''spastic'', in which the attempt to write excites clonic or tonic contractions of the fingers; ''tremulous'', in which the hand shakes so while writing that the letters formed are indistinguishable; and ''sensory'', in which the effort to write causes severe pain, tingling, or other abnormal sensations in the hand and at times in the forearm also. The symptoms vary greatly in different individuals, usually, however, increasing in severity as long as the attempt to use a pen is persisted in. The use of steel pens and metal penholders is supposed to increase the liability to the affection. Also called ''scriveners’ cramp'' or ''palsy'', ''writers’ palsy'' or ''paralysis'', and ''graphospasm''.—'''Writers to the signet.''' See ''signet'', 1.}}

'''writeress''' (rī′tėr-es), ''n.''   [< ''writer'' + ''-ess''.]   A female writer or author. [Humorous.]
{{smaller block|Remember it henceforth, ye ''writeresses'', there is no such word as authoress.
{{right|''Thackeray'', Misc., ii. 470. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''writerling''' (rī′tėr-ling), ''n.''   [< ''writer'' + ''-ling''<sup>1</sup>.]   A petty or sorry writer or author. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Every writer and ''writerling'' of name [in France] has a salary from the government.
{{right|''W. Taylor'', 1802 (Robberds’s Memoir, I. 420). (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''writership''' (rī′tėr-ship), ''n.''   [< ''writer'' + ''-ship''.]   The office or employment of a writer in some official capacity.

'''writhe''' (rīᴛ̵ʜ), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''writhed'', ppr. ''writhing''.   [< ME. ''writhen'', ''wrythen'' (pret. ''wroth'', ''wrooth'', ''wræth'', pl. ''writhen'', pp. ''writhen'' (with short ''i''), ''wrethen''), < AS. ''wrīthan'' (pret. ''wrāth'', pp. ''writhen''), twist, wind about, = OHG. ''rīdan'', MHG. ''rīden'', G. dial. ''wrideln'', twist together, = Icel. ''ritha'' = Sw. ''vrida'' = Dan. ''vride'', wring, twist, turn, wrest. Hence ult. ''wreath'', ''wrest'', ''wrist''.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To turn and twist about; twist out of shape or position; wrench; contort.
{{smaller block|<poem>The stortes [grape-stalks] softe in handes wol thai take
And ''writhe'' hem, and so ''writhen'' wol thai lete
Hem honge and drie awhile in sonnes hete.</poem>
{{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 206.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Sa suld we ''wryth'' all syn away,
That in our breistis bred.</poem>
{{right|''The Bludy Serk'' (Child’s Ballads, VIII. 151).}}}}
{{smaller block|The desolate little shanty was plainly to be seen among the naked and ''writhen'' boughs of the orchard.
{{right|''The Atlantic'', LVIII. 389.}}}}
'''2.''' To wrest perversely; wrest; pervert.
{{smaller block|The reason which he yieldeth showeth the least part of his meaning to be that whereunto his words are ''writhed.''
{{right|''Hooker.''}}}}
'''3.''' To wrench; wring; extort. [Obsolete or archaic.]
{{smaller block|The nobility hesitated not to follow the example of their sovereign in ''writhing'' money from them by every species of oppression.
{{right|''Scott'', Ivanhoe, vi. (''Imp. Dict.'')}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To move or stir in a twisting or tortuous manner; twist about, as from pain, distress, or stimulation. {{smaller block|The poplar ''writhes'' and twists and whistles in the blast.
{{right|''Irving'', Knickerbocker, p. 185.}}}}

{{smaller block|Supposing a case of tyranny, the Tuscans will wriggle under it rather than ''writhe;'' and if even they should ''writhe'', yet they will never stand erect. {{right|''Landor.''}}}}

{{smaller block|She ''writhed'' under the demonstrable truth of the character he had given her conduct.
{{right|''George Eliot'', Mill on the Floss, v. 5.}}}}

{{smaller block|The ''writhing'' worm . . . failed to allure the scaly brood.
{{right|''Geikie'', Geol. Sketches, i.}}}}

'''writhe''' (rīᴛ̵ʜ), ''n.''   [< ''writhe'', ''v.'']   '''1.''' A contortion of form or features, as from pain or other emotion; an act of writhing. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Perhaps pleasure is the emotion evidenced by the silent ''writhe'' with which Jim receives this piece of information.
{{right|''R. Broughton'', Alas, xvi.}}}}
'''2.''' The band of a fagot. ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
